name: PT Bank Victoria International Tbk

frontmatter.title: Bank Victoria International — a sub-scale bank priced for a return it does not earn
frontmatter.summary: Bank Victoria is a controlled, sub-scale Jakarta bank earning a low-single-digit return on equity, paying no dividend, and trading at a multiple of book that requires a return it has not delivered in years. The balance sheet is well capitalised and the controlling shareholder has just bought stock above the market, but neither route puts cash into a minority's hands. Sell, target Rp37.
thesis: The bank earns a low-single-digit return on equity on an over-capitalised balance sheet; at a cost of equity of 12.9% that return is worth a small fraction of book, not a premium to it.

Non-interest income is the swing factor and it has collapsed — the first nine months of 2026 booked a fraction of the prior year's other operating income, and the company's own plan assumes it returns.
Growth is not the constraint. Loans are a little over three-fifths of assets, the rest is a securities book funded with wholesale money, and the loan book has been shrinking while the system grows.
No dividend was declared at either of the last two annual meetings, so the minority's expected return is book-value compounding below the cost of equity, with no cash return for waiting.

The price already capitalises a return on equity of about five per cent, against 3.6% modelled for the mid-cycle and a FY2025 return of 3.4%; that gap, not the bank's asset quality, is the mispricing.

Control is the counter-argument and it belongs in the bull case — the controlling shareholder bought shares at a premium to the market in November 2026, and a tender offer or capital action would change the arithmetic for minorities. Nothing in the record commits to one.

catalysts.event: November 2026 monthly publication: whether the fourth-quarter loan book and deposit base stabilise after the nine-month contraction
Full-year 2026 audited results: the level of non-interest income ex-one-offs and the size of the fourth-quarter provisioning charge
Annual general meeting: whether FY2026 earnings are retained again after two consecutive zero-dividend meetings
Any IDX or OJK filing following Victoria Investama's November purchase, including a tender or restructuring proposal
OJK monthly banking data: system loan and deposit growth against the bank's own trajectory

blocks.text: **SELL, target Rp37 against a price of Rp72, a total return of -48.8%.** The call is not that Bank Victoria is about to fail. It is that the price asks a sub-scale bank to earn a return it has not earned in years, while the capital that could lift that return sits on the balance sheet with no stated route back to minorities. The bank reported net profit of IDR131.7bn in FY2025 on equity of IDR4,368.9bn, a return on equity of 3.4% on the company's own measure [S4]. Nine months into FY2026 the profit is IDR101.0bn, below the prior year, and the loan book has contracted [S8][S9].

The variant view is about where the value comes from. The market is not paying for the earnings stream: at 0.3x of FY2026E book, the price capitalises a sustainable return on equity well above the 3.6% our model uses — an implied five per cent, which the bank last earned in 2022 [S7]. What the price can be defended on is the balance sheet — a capital adequacy ratio of 23.8% and a loan book worth IDR22,380.2bn against a market capitalisation of IDR1,326.2bn [S4][S0]. That is a control or asset value, and a minority holder cannot monetise it without a distribution, a tender or a sale. The controlling shareholder's November purchase at Rp80 shows what a strategic buyer pays; it does not set a floor under the shares a minority owns [S5].

What moves the value, in order: the sustainable return on equity (driven by non-interest income recovery and credit cost), the cost of equity, and any corporate action. Our base case has the bank earning 1.9% on equity in FY2026E and 3.8% by FY2030E, still far below the 12.9% cost of equity, and paying nothing. The weighted target is Rp37; the bull case, which requires a capital action or a much stronger recovery, reaches Rp86. That is the honest shape of the bet: the downside is the arithmetic, the upside is corporate.

Bank Victoria International is a commercial bank listed on the Indonesia Stock Exchange and controlled by PT Victoria Investama, which holds 64.2% of the voting rights after its November 2026 purchase [S5]. It is a conventional bank only: the remaining stake in Bank Victoria Syariah was sold in FY2025, a transaction that produced a one-off gain of IDR100.7bn inside other operating income [S7]. The bank employs 736.0 people and operates from Jakarta with a branch network serving corporate, commercial and consumer customers [S0][S4].

The balance sheet is best understood as two books. The first is the loan book, IDR22,380.2bn gross at the end of FY2025 and IDR21,382.4bn at September 2026, down over the nine months as the bank ran off wholesale funding rather than chasing volume [S7][S8]. The second is a securities book of IDR8,627.5bn at September 2026, funded by customer deposits of IDR24,294.7bn at end-FY2025 and IDR3,548.2bn of current accounts, IDR3,885.1bn of savings and IDR16,143.5bn of time deposits at September 2026, alongside IDR3,977.0bn of securities the bank has issued [S8]. On the funding side the mix is the story: time deposits are the majority of the base, and the low-cost share is 29.3% [S4]. On the asset side, loans are a little over three-fifths of total assets, which is why the margin is thin and why a securities book priced off the sovereign curve matters as much as lending [S8].

Revenue comes from three places. Net interest income was IDR555.6bn in FY2025 [S7], fees and administration income IDR99.1bn in the first nine months of FY2026 [S8], and other operating income — trading, recoveries of written-off assets, dividend and the one-off Syariah gain — the balance [S7]. The fee franchise is small relative to the book, which is characteristic of a bank that lends to small and medium enterprises rather than running a transaction-banking franchise.

Strategy is set out in the company's business plan for the 2026-2028 period: organic loan growth in productive segments, funding-cost discipline through CASA, digital-channel investment and group synergies [S4]. The plan's own numbers are ambitious against the run-rate: profit before tax of IDR224.0bn and net profit of IDR175.0bn for FY2026, on third-party funds of IDR25,702.0bn [S4]. Nine months in, profit before tax is IDR134.6bn [S8], so the plan requires a fourth quarter far above anything the first three delivered.

Competitive position is the weak link. The bank is sub-scale against a system whose loans grew 13.3% year on year to September 2026 while Bank Victoria's own book shrank [S10][S11]. It has no structural cost advantage, no large low-cost deposit franchise and no dominant product; it competes for deposits on price and for assets on relationship and speed. That is a viable niche for a well-run small bank, but it is not a franchise that supports a premium to book when the return on equity is in the low single digits.

The Indonesian banking system is large, growing and concentrated. OJK reported system loans growing 13.3% year on year at September 2026 and third-party funds growing 8.2% [S10][S11]. Growth is decelerating — the same release puts the prior month's loan growth higher — but it remains double-digit, and it is being led by investment and corporate credit rather than consumption [S10][S12]. That composition matters for a bank like Bank Victoria: the fastest-growing segments are exactly where the large corporate banks have the relationships, the balance sheet and the pricing power.

The macro backdrop is a cautious one. The house view has Bank Indonesia's policy rate easing only gradually, inflation running around three per cent [S0], and a rupiah that remains sensitive to the global rate cycle. For a bank, that translates into a deposit market that stays competitive: when policy rates are high and liquidity is not abundant, time-deposit rates do not fall as fast as loan yields, and the margin compresses. The system's deposit growth trailing loan growth by several points [S11] is the mechanism — banks bid for funds.

Regulation is both barrier and cost. OJK sets capital adequacy, liquidity and provisioning rules under the POJK framework; PSAK 71 requires expected-credit-loss provisioning, which front-loads credit cost when a book deteriorates; and the bank's capital category determines which activities it can undertake at what intensity. The practical consequence for a small bank is that compliance and technology spending are largely fixed, so the cost-to-income ratio is structurally higher than for a large bank — Bank Victoria's own ratio was 48.4% in FY2025 and deteriorated in the nine months to September 2026 as income fell [S4][S8].

Competition is intense at both ends. At the top, the large private and state banks have the CASA franchise, the corporate relationships and the funding cost; the state banks grew faster than the system in the latest OJK data [S10]. At the bottom, digital banks and multifinance companies compete for the same SME and consumer borrowers with faster turnaround and, in several cases, a lower cost base. Bank Victoria sits in the middle: too small to set price, too large to be a niche specialist. Its response has been to lean on group synergies and to hold a large securities book, which supports liquidity and capital but earns a spread close to the sovereign curve [S4][S8].

The five forces are unfavourable on four of five [S0][S4][S10]. Rivalry among banks is high and price-based; the power of depositors is high because switching costs are low and deposit insurance makes all banks close substitutes up to the insured limit; the threat of new entrants is moderate in banking licences but high in the digital wallets and lending platforms that intercept the customer; the power of borrowers is moderate but rising as credit data improves. Only regulation, which restricts entry and sets a capital floor, works in the incumbent's favour — and it also caps returns by requiring capital the bank cannot deploy at a spread.

The moat question has a short answer, and it is no: there is no durable moat. The bank's assets are commodity loans and securities, its funding is largely price-sensitive time deposits, and its fee income is small. That is not a reason to dismiss the equity — a cheap enough price can compensate — but it is a reason to insist that the valuation rest on the earnings the bank actually produces, not on a franchise premium [S7][S8][S10].

The five-year record is one of a bank that has not earned its cost of capital. Net interest income was IDR544.5bn in FY2024 and IDR555.6bn in FY2025; other operating income IDR9.3bn and IDR304.9bn on the model's line, with the caveat in the data note below; provisions IDR202.0bn and IDR308.3bn; and net profit IDR117.9bn and IDR131.7bn [S7]. Equity rose from IDR3,933.5bn to IDR4,368.9bn, so the return on equity stayed in the low single digits even as absolute profit grew [S7][S4]. Book value per share fell in FY2025 despite the profit, because the share count rose: the Series VII warrants were exercised during the year, adding shares at par and diluting book value per share [S7].

The FY2026 picture is the hinge. Nine-month net interest income was IDR538.2bn against IDR372.9bn a year earlier, a large increase driven by a fall in interest expense while interest income rose [S8][S9]. That is a genuine funding-cost gain, not an accounting one, and it is the reason the full-year net interest income forecast of IDR717.5bn is well above FY2025. But other operating income collapsed: IDR533.3bn in FY2025 included the IDR100.7bn Syariah gain, and the nine months of FY2026 booked a fraction of the prior year's total [S7][S8][S9]. The result is that pre-provision profit of IDR429.5bn is absorbed by provisions of IDR308.6bn and other charges, leaving profit before tax of IDR110.8bn, tax of IDR27.7bn and net profit of IDR83.1bn — barely above FY2025 despite the much stronger net interest line [S7][S8].

Against the company's own plan that gap is large, and it is worth reconciling on the plan's own lines. The RBB for 2026 projects net interest income of IDR579.0bn, net operating income and expense other than interest of IDR-308.0bn, operating profit of IDR270.0bn, net non-operating income and expense of IDR-47.0bn and profit before tax of IDR224.0bn, with net profit of IDR175.0bn [S4]. What the plan does not contain is a provisioning line: its summary profit statement runs from net interest income through operating profit to profit before tax without a credit charge, so the 2026 plan is written with essentially no provisioning for the year [S4]. Nine months in, profit before tax is IDR134.6bn [S8], so the plan needs a fourth quarter well above the nine-month run-rate. Our model is above the plan on the operating lines — net interest income of IDR717.5bn against IDR579.0bn, because the funding-cost gain in the nine-month actual is stronger than the plan assumed, and non-interest income of IDR220.1bn less operating expenses of IDR508.2bn against the plan's IDR-308.0bn — so the whole gap to the plan's profit before tax is the credit charge. We carry FY2026E provisions of IDR308.6bn where the plan carries essentially none, which takes profit before tax to IDR110.8bn and net profit to IDR83.1bn against IDR224.0bn and IDR175.0bn [S4]. Our base case does not grant the fourth quarter the plan requires, because the audited pattern says the fourth quarter carries the true-up: the FY2025 charge was IDR308.3bn against IDR180.9bn in the first nine months of that year [S7][S9], and we repeat that shape in FY2026E. Even annualising the nine-month charge of IDR180.3bn and granting no fourth-quarter true-up at all leaves profit before tax below the plan line, because the plan is not carrying the credit charge in the first place; that no-true-up case is the bull branch, not the base case.

Our forecast has revenue growing modestly from here. Net interest income reaches IDR739.7bn in FY2027E and IDR895.7bn by FY2030E as loans resume growing at a below-system rate and the margin grinds slightly higher on a better CASA mix. Non-interest income recovers to IDR275.2bn in FY2027E and IDR333.9bn in FY2030E, which is still below the FY2025 LK figure net of the one-off. Total operating income of IDR937.7bn in FY2026E rises to IDR1,229.6bn by FY2030E. Operating expenses at a cost-to-income ratio of 54.2% consume IDR508.2bn in FY2026E, leaving pre-provision profit of IDR429.5bn. Provisions at a credit cost of 1.4% take IDR308.6bn, and other non-operating items a small net charge [S0].

The balance sheet follows the plan rather than the market. Loans of IDR21,395.4bn in FY2026E grow to IDR26,756.4bn; deposits of IDR23,590.2bn to IDR29,501.1bn; the loan-to-deposit ratio stays near 90.7%, which is close to the reported FY2025 level of 92.1% [S4]. On the same five-year horizon equity compounds at the retained profit — IDR4,452.1bn to IDR5,078.6bn, with no dividend — and book value per share goes from Rp242 to Rp276, with the estimated capital ratio falling from 21.7% to 19.8%. Beyond that horizon the terminal payout slows equity growth against a growing loan book: by FY2035E book value per share is Rp306 and the estimated capital ratio 17.2%, still far above the regulatory minimum, while the reported end-FY2025 ratio of 23.8% is higher than the FY2026E estimate because that measure includes supplementary capital [S4][S0]. The bank has no capital constraint; it has a deployment problem.

Margins and credit cost are where the model could be wrong in either direction. The margin is measured over average total assets, not the company's narrower earning-asset base, so it reads lower than the reported 2.0%; the net interest income level is anchored on the nine-month actual, so the denominator choice does not change the profit [S4][S8]. Credit cost of 1.4% is the number that decides FY2026E, and it is not the nine-month run-rate. The nine months charged IDR180.3bn on average loans of about IDR21,382.4bn, an annualised rate of one point one per cent; the audited FY2025 charged IDR308.3bn, or one point four four per cent, against IDR180.9bn in the first nine months of 2025 [S7][S9], so well over a third of the year's charge landed in the fourth quarter, because the nine-month charge was almost unchanged year on year while the full-year charge was not. Assuming the nine-month rate holds for the year would repeat exactly the error the audited accounts expose, so the base case annualises the nine-month charge and adds a fourth quarter at the FY2025 Q4 level, which is the 1.4% above and about IDR308.6bn of provisions — a repeat of the true-up costs roughly a third of FY2026E net profit against the nine-month run-rate. From FY2027E the assumption glides to 1.2%: the direction of the classified stock supports it, since gross NPL fell from 3.3% to 2.5% and restructured loans fell to IDR1,874.5bn [S7][S4]. The valid reading of the asset-quality data is not that a hidden stock is growing — it fell — but that the charge rose from IDR202.0bn to IDR308.3bn while the classified stock shrank, i.e. the bank is provisioning above its flow, and a fourth-quarter true-up is a recurring feature of the audited year rather than a one-off.

Capital allocation is simple and shareholder-unfriendly. Dividends per share were Rp0.0 for FY2025 and the annual meetings of 2024 and 2025 resolved not to distribute [S4], so retained earnings accumulate in equity that earns a low return. The company's own FY2026 plan carries zero distributed dividends [S4]. The one capital event in the record is dilutive: the warrant exercise lifted the share count at par, transferring value from existing holders to the warrant holders [S7]. There is no buyback, no special dividend and no stated plan to return the capital that the loan book cannot use.

Earnings quality, in the terms of the house screen, has three flags. First, the one-off: the Syariah disposal gain of IDR100.7bn flattered FY2025 other operating income and does not repeat [S7]. Second, the provisioning trend: the charge rose from IDR202.0bn to IDR308.3bn while the classified stock fell — gross NPL from 3.3% to 2.5% and restructured loans to IDR1,874.5bn — which is provisioning ahead of the flow, the opposite of borrowing earnings from the future, though the fourth-quarter concentration means the quarterly run-rate understates the annual charge [S7][S4]. Third, the equity base includes a fixed-asset revaluation surplus of IDR299.3bn, so the book value used in the multiple is not all cash-generating capital [S7]. On the positive side the audit opinion is unmodified, signed by KAP Purwanto Susanti dan Surja (an Ernst & Young member firm), and the related-party loan book is small — IDR219.6bn, about one per cent of loans — though it grew sharply in FY2025 [S7][S4]. A bank's accrual ratio is not meaningful; the provisioning and classification trends are the equivalent test, and they are adequate rather than clean.

A general point about small Indonesian banks frames the numbers above. The sector's returns are
structurally dispersed: the largest banks earn a return on equity well above their cost of capital on a
low-cost deposit franchise, while the smallest earn a thin spread on a book funded by price-sensitive
time deposits and carry a fixed cost base that does not scale. Consolidation has been the regulator's
preferred answer for a decade, and a small bank with excess capital is a natural seller or merger
partner. None of that is a forecast about this bank; it is the reason the multiple, not the earnings, is
where the argument happens.

**Data note — the pack-to-LK bridge.** The data pack's historical non-interest-income line is narrower than the audited income statement, and the model's history is the pack's. For FY2025 the pack shows IDR555.6bn of net interest income against the LK's IDR558.7bn [S7], and IDR304.9bn of non-interest income against the LK's other operating income of IDR533.3bn [S7]; total operating income on the pack basis is therefore IDR860.5bn against the LK's one trillion and ninety-two billion, a gap of about a fifth that is entirely classification, not economics. The bottom line closes: the pack's profit before tax (IDR162.4bn) and net profit (IDR131.7bn) are the audited figures, as are equity and the provision charge, so the return-on-equity calibration and every valuation input are unaffected. The same classification difference is present and larger in FY2024: the pack carries IDR9.3bn of non-interest income against the LK's IDR365.7bn [S7], while its net profit of IDR117.9bn is again the audited bottom line, so the two-year history is consistent at the profit line even where the classification line is not. What is affected is any growth rate computed off the pack line: the reported decline in FY2026E non-interest income is a basis bridge from the pack's narrow FY2025 line to a IDR220.1bn forecast that is anchored on the LK's nine-month actual (IDR99.1bn of fees plus other income) [S8], and it is not an economic decline of that size. On the LK's own basis, other operating income was IDR533.3bn in FY2025 including the IDR100.7bn Syariah disposal gain and IDR220.1bn is forecast for FY2026E — a fall of roughly half, which is the number to hold in mind. A second denominator difference remains: the model measures the margin on average total assets while the company reports NIM on a narrower earning-asset base (2.0% for FY2025) [S4]; the net interest income line itself is tied to the reported actuals.

A bank is valued on its equity, not on enterprise value: deposits and borrowings are raw material, not leverage, and the cash on the balance sheet is the liquidity buffer that keeps the loan book running. The two methods that fit are therefore the warranted price-to-book multiple — what the market should pay for a given sustainable return on equity against the cost of equity — and a residual-income run, which charges the cost of equity against every year of retained book and capitalises the shortfall. A dividend discount model does not fit: the payout is zero [S4].

The cost of equity is 12.9% and the weighted average cost of capital is the same, because there is no debt weight in an equity valuation [S0]. The engine applies the CAPM in one line: (7.4% sovereign yield less its 1.6% default spread) plus 0.90 of levered beta applied to the sum of the mature-market equity risk premium of 4.2% and the country risk premium of 2.5%, plus an explicit premium of 1.0%, which gives 12.9% [S0]. The beta therefore multiplies the equity and country premia together — not the equity premium alone — and the country premium sits inside the beta-adjusted term, so the printed cost of equity is reproducible from these five inputs. The premium is the gap between the engine's unpinned CAPM arithmetic and the method card's pinned build — the sovereign yield plus an IDR equity risk premium at the mid-point of the house band — not a size or illiquidity charge. The only marketability adjustment is the liquidity discount applied to the target, which is material because average daily turnover is IDR0.2bn [S0].

The warranted multiple and the residual-income run now rest on one terminal assumption. The sustainable return on equity is 3.60%, the mid-cycle average of the model's own path from 1.88% in FY2026E to 4.56% in FY2035E — not the trough and not the last year, but the return the bank's operating build produces once the 2026 provisioning true-up is past. Terminal growth is 1.64% and the terminal payout is 55.00%, and the three are arithmetically tied: growth equals the sustainable return on equity times one minus the payout. The multiple is 17.5% of book, applied to the opening book value per share — equity of IDR4,437.0bn at 30 September 2026 [S8] over 18,419.4m shares [S7], which is the opening capital the residual-income run also uses — giving Rp42. The FY2025A book of Rp237 is the older line and is not the basis: the nine months of 2026 added profit to the book, so the FY2025A figure understates the opening capital by that result net of other movements, and pairing it with the ratio would not reproduce the value. The residual-income run, which charges the cost of equity against every year of the ramp and capitalises the shortfall, gives Rp30 — -28.3% relative to the multiple. The gap is not a disagreement about the terminal bank; it is the present value of the transition, which the single ratio cannot see. We weight residual income at 60.0% because it is the method card's engine and the only method that prices the path, the warranted multiple at 40.0% as the check that the terminal is priced consistently, and give the dividend model nothing [S0].

Terminal growth is the parameter that decides whether the answer is small or absurd, and it is derived rather than asserted. We use 1.64%, below the house default, and the reason is the Gordon constraint: terminal growth cannot exceed the sustainable return on equity times one minus the payout. With a sustainable return of 3.60% and a terminal payout of 55.00% — retention of the balance — the bound is the product of those two inputs. The model carries 1.64%: that is the product computed on the unrounded ten-year mean return, while the same expression on the rounded input comes out two basis points lower, which is rounding rather than a second assumption. The forecast pays nothing through FY2029E because the company's meetings resolved against a dividend [S4]; the terminal payout is the steady state the frame requires, not a forecast that a particular annual meeting votes one. The earlier version of this model set g at two per cent against a stated half-earnings payout while paying nothing forever, which is arithmetically impossible: a bank that never distributes has a Gordon value of zero whatever return it earns, and a bank that grows at two per cent off a four per cent return must distribute about half. The two cases bracket the answer, and the sensitivity table shows both.

Capital and the bridge deserve a paragraph because this is a bank and the arithmetic is different. The engine applies no bridge, and that is correct: a bank's cash is an operating asset, not a distributable surplus. The capital that could be returned is the equity above the regulatory minimum, and the bank has a great deal of it: core capital of IDR4,000.4bn against nine per cent of total risk-weighted assets of IDR21,514.1bn leaves a surplus larger than the bank's entire market capitalisation of IDR1,326.2bn [S4][S0] — the number the bull branch would be about if it were funded. That is the point the residual-income method cannot express: it assumes the capital is retained forever at a low return. There is no announcement of a distribution in the archived record, which is why it is not in the base case. The post-balance-sheet search to 13 November 2026 changes nothing in the bridge: it found the controller's 9 November purchase at Rp80 [S5], the exchange's rise in the minimum free float to 15.0% [S13] and the MSCI consultation on Indonesia's market classification [S14], and none of the three is a distributable item, a capital action or a contingent payment, so the bridge stays empty.

What today's price implies is the cleanest statement of the mispricing. At Rp72 the shares trade at 0.3x of FY2026E book. Holding our cost of equity of 12.9% and terminal growth of 1.6%, inverting the warranted multiple at that ratio gives an implied sustainable return on equity of five per cent — the terminal growth plus the traded multiple times the spread between the cost of equity and that growth, so the figure moves with the inputs printed here. That is well above the 3.6% we model for the mid-cycle and above even the 4.6% terminal return [S0][S7]. The market is not pricing the bank that exists; it is pricing a bank that earns a normal return on its capital, or one whose capital will be returned at close to book. The first is not supported by the accounts; the second is a corporate event, not an earnings forecast.

The bull case is real and we do not bury it, but it has two branches and only one is in the weighted target. The operating branch is what the scenario prices: the mirror of the bear on credit cost, margin and growth, reaching Rp86 with the share count held flat, because a buyback or distribution has to be funded and an unfunded per-share uplift would be free money. The corporate branch is a transaction, and it is worth stating plainly: the controller paid Rp80 per share in November 2026 [S5], a third of book; a tender or merger at book would be worth Rp237 — more than five times our target. That branch is not in the engine's scenario set, because the engine shocks operating drivers and cannot price a bid; it is also binary and unsourced, and the last capital event, the warrant exercise, diluted rather than distributed [S7]. Our bull is therefore a fundamental value, not a control value, and if anything it truncates the upside rather than flattering it. A filed tender at or above the controller's own purchase price would change the rating regardless of the fundamental value.

The weighted target is Rp46 before the liquidity discount of 20.0%, giving Rp37 against a price of Rp72, a total return of -48.8% [S0]. The return is computed on the engine's unrounded discounted target, which rounds to the price shown, so it is not the arithmetic of the rounded figure.

The main downside risk is not a credit event; it is the persistence of the current arithmetic. A return on equity of 3.2% against a cost of equity of 12.9% means every year the bank retains earnings it transfers value from shareholders to borrowers, depositors and staff, and the transfer compounds [S0][S4]. Likelihood high, impact high — this is the base case, not the tail.

The second risk is credit, and it is a genuine unknown rather than a modelled certainty. Gross NPL of 2.5% looks manageable, but IDR879.9bn of loans sat in special mention at end-FY2025 and IDR1,874.5bn were still restructured — a stock larger than the NPL line and not yet charged [S7]. If that book migrates, credit cost roughly doubles in our model and the return on equity falls toward zero. Likelihood medium, impact high.

The third risk is funding and margin. Time deposits are IDR16,143.5bn — roughly two thirds of customer deposits at the September 2026 mark, on a loan book of IDR21,382.4bn [S8] — so the margin is highly sensitive to deposit competition, and the 2026 improvement in net interest income came from funding costs falling — a gain that can reverse [S8][S9]. A sharper squeeze than our base case is the bear scenario. Likelihood medium, impact material.

The third-and-a-half risk is the securities book, and it is the largest unmodeled exposure on the balance sheet. Securities held were IDR8,627.5bn at September 2026, a quarter of assets and almost twice equity, carried at fair value, against IDR3,977.0bn of securities the bank has issued on the funding side [S8]. A five per cent adverse revaluation is about a tenth of equity, and a repricing of the issued bonds adds the funding leg; the model has no mark-to-market line, so this sits outside the scenarios and inside the risk list. It does not change the base case, where the book is largely government and short-dated paper, but it is why we would not call the equity an asset-value floor without checking the composition first.

The fourth risk is regulatory and capital. A small bank with a high capital ratio but a low return may be pushed by the regulator toward consolidation, or may be required to raise capital it does not need; a discounted rights issue would dilute book value per share and is the standard mechanism for small Indonesian banks. Nothing in the record says it will happen, and the CAR of 23.8% means there is no need for one, so it sits in the bear case. Likelihood low, impact high.

The fifth risk is governance and related parties. Loans to related parties rose sharply in FY2025 to IDR219.6bn, small in absolute terms but a reminder that the controlling shareholder sets the terms [S4]. The controller holds 64.2% and the free float is 17.9% [S5][S0], so the minority cannot force a distribution or block a transaction that is fair to the controller but not to them. Likelihood medium, impact medium.

The sixth risk is liquidity, and it cuts the other way. Average daily turnover of IDR0.2bn means a position cannot be exited in size without moving the price, which is why the house applies a liquidity discount to the target [S0]. It also means the shares can trade far from value for long periods, in either direction, without a fundamental catalyst.

The counter-argument that deserves the most space is the controller's own buying. Victoria Investama raised its voting stake to 64.2% in November 2026 at Rp80, a premium to the market [S5]. A strategic buyer with full information paying above the market is evidence that the assets have value; it is not evidence that the price will converge to that value for a minority. Control is worth more per share than a minority stake — it can direct the balance sheet, appoint the board and choose the timing of any distribution. If the purchase is the first step toward a tender offer or a merger at or above that price, our call is wrong, and the bull case is where that outcome lives. We would change the rating on a filed tender, not on the purchase alone.

The three scenarios are mirrored in their drivers, as the house requires. Bear: credit cost sixty basis points higher, margin forty basis points lower and loan growth three points lower, with the share count held flat; the three together take the first forecast year into a loss — the base pre-tax profit does not cover the combined hit — and keep the return on equity at about one per cent for a decade, so on a going-concern basis the equity is worth Rp19. That is not a zero, but it is close to one, and the asset value is higher: marking loans down fifteen per cent and the securities book five per cent leaves a liquidation value in the region of a third of book, which is what a controller who chose to sell or wind up would realise, and is the true floor under a solvent bank with a 23.8% capital ratio. We do not put that floor in the bear because it requires a decision the controller has not signalled; it is the other side of the bet. Base: the most probable path, the one built in section three, with non-interest income recovering only to a fraction of its FY2025 level. Bull: the exact mirror on the operating drivers with a flat share count, bringing the return on equity toward six per cent and a value of Rp86. The values are not mirrored even though the shocks are: the residual-income method is convex in the return on equity against a fixed equity charge, so the bull gains more than the bear loses, and the bear is weighted at 25.0% rather than more. That asymmetry is a property of the frame, not of the weights.

Signposts that would change the view, in order of importance: a filed tender offer or merger at a price above the market; a declared dividend or capital-return plan; a return on equity above five per cent for two consecutive halves without a capital raise, which would require non-interest income to recover much faster than our base; and a fall in special-mention and restructured loans that would let credit cost drop below our assumption [S7][S8]. Any of the first two would move the rating toward neutral regardless of the fundamental value, because they change what a minority can actually receive.

Ownership is concentrated and explains much of the valuation. PT Victoria Investama holds 64.2% of the voting rights after its November 2026 purchase [S5], and the shares in free float are 17.9% [S0]. Those are the two figures this report uses, and they are not complements: the controller's block sits outside the float, and the rest of the register between them belongs to non-controller institutions and individuals whose shares the data provider does not count as free float. The data pack also publishes an insider percentage, but it is struck on a different basis — it counts the controller inside it and overlaps the free-float cut — and the archived record does not identify which holders appear in both, so it is neither additive to the float nor a separate holder class, and we do not use it. On the two sourced figures the register is tightly held, with the free float at 17.9% against a controller at 64.2%. Free float is now a live constraint, not a footnote: the exchange has raised its minimum free float from seven and a half to 15.0% [S13], and the MSCI consultation on Indonesia's market classification is explicitly about ownership concentration and investability [S14]. A further purchase by the controller pushes the float toward that floor and forces either a sell-down or exclusion from indices — a governance risk with a price effect, and one we would treat as a signpost.

Related-party exposure is modest but rising. Loans to related parties were IDR219.6bn at end-FY2025, up sharply on the prior year, against third-party loans of IDR22,160.0bn [S4]. At around one per cent of the book this is not a value-destruction channel on the scale seen elsewhere on the exchange, but it is the direction of travel that matters, and it should be monitored through the annual-report related-party note.

The auditor is KAP Purwanto Susanti dan Surja, an Ernst & Young member firm, and the FY2025 opinion is unmodified [S7]. The financial statements are prepared under Indonesian GAAP with PSAK 71 provisioning. Two accounting items deserve a flag rather than a red card. First, equity includes a fixed-asset revaluation surplus of IDR299.3bn, which inflates book value relative to cash-generating capital; a pre-revaluation book value would make the multiple we pay look slightly higher, not lower [S7]. Second, the warrant exercise in FY2025 added shares at par, diluting book value per share in a year the bank reported a profit [S7]. Both are disclosed, so they are optics-class, not manipulation-class, but they mean the book value in the multiple is not a clean measure of shareholder capital.

Dividend policy is the governance fact that matters most for the valuation. Dividends per share were Rp0.0 for FY2025, and the annual meetings of 2024 and 2025 both resolved not to distribute [S4]. The company's own plan carries zero distributed dividends [S4]. A minority holder is therefore relying entirely on capital appreciation, which requires either a re-rating the earnings do not support or a corporate action the controller has not announced.

ESG disclosure is at the level OJK and the exchange require, through the sustainability report published with the annual report [S4]. The bank's direct environmental footprint is small — offices and data — and its material exposures are social and governance: responsible lending to SME borrowers, customer data protection and the concentration of control. We found no ESG-related enforcement or controversy in the archived sources [S5][S10][S11][S12], and we make no claim beyond that; the absence of a finding in a limited search is not a clean bill of health.

The near-term calendar is thin, which is itself part of the investment case: there is no scheduled event that forces a re-rating. The monthly publication for November 2026 will show whether the loan book and deposit base stabilise after the nine-month contraction [S8]. The full-year 2026 audited accounts, due by the end of the first quarter, will settle two questions: the sustainable level of non-interest income excluding the Syariah gain, and the size of the fourth-quarter provisioning charge [S3]. The annual general meeting in the middle of 2027 will decide again whether any of the FY2026 profit is paid out [S4]. Any IDX or OJK filing following the November purchase — a tender, a merger or a capital action — is the single event that would change the rating [S5]. On the industry side, the monthly OJK banking data give the system loan and deposit growth against which the bank's own trajectory should be judged [S10].

The KPIs we watch, in order: non-interest income excluding one-offs; the cost-to-income ratio; credit cost and the special-mention and restructured balances; CASA and the loan-to-deposit ratio; and any change in the share count or dividend policy. The first and the last are the ones that would move the value materially; the middle three are the ones that would move the earnings [S4][S7][S8].

bear.narrative: The 2026 non-interest-income collapse proves structural rather than lumpy: fee and recovery income does not return, the loan book keeps shrinking as the bank runs off wholesale funding, and the fourth-quarter true-up is not a one-off. Credit cost is sixty basis points higher for the whole forecast, margin forty basis points lower as time-deposit competition returns, and loan growth three points lower. Those three add to a first-year loss - the base case pre-tax profit does not cover the combined hit - and keep the return on equity at about one per cent for a decade, far below the cost of equity; on a going-concern residual-income basis, and with the share count held flat, the equity is worth nothing. The asset value is the only floor: marking loans down and the securities book a little leaves something, but it is a liquidation value the controller would have to choose, not an operating outcome.

bull.narrative: The mirror of the bear on the same three drivers: credit cost sixty basis points lower as the restructured book cures, NIM forty basis points higher as CASA passes a third of deposits and the wholesale bonds are refinanced (that is 2.55%, still at the 2023 reported margin [S4]), and loan growth three points higher on group-synergy lending. The share count is held flat: the capital return is carried in the narrative, not as a free per-share uplift, because a buyback or special distribution has to be funded and no filing commits to one. The observed controller price of Rp80 [S5] and a transaction at book value are corporate outcomes, priced separately in section 4 and not inside this operating scenario.

assumptions.label: Loan growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E -4.4% is the actual: gross loans were Rp21.38tn at 30 September 2026 against Rp22.38tn at 31 December 2025, a 4.5% contraction in the first nine months [F3][F2], and we carry that into a flat fourth quarter. The bank is shrinking while the system grows 13.26% [S11]; the reason is visible in the balance sheet, not in a demand story - it is running down wholesale funding rather than growing the loan book [S8]. From FY2027E 5-6% is a below-system recovery consistent with the RBB 2026-2028 plan of organic growth supported by group synergies [S4], still far below the 13% industry rate. No haircut is applied to the recovery: it is slower than the industry because the bank is sub-scale and KBMI 1, not because we assume the worst.

assumptions.label: Deposit growth
assumptions.basis: FY2026E -2.9%: customer deposits were Rp23.58tn at 30 September 2026 - giro Rp3.55tn, tabungan Rp3.89tn, deposito Rp16.14tn [F6][F7][F8] - against Rp24.29tn at end-2025 [F5], and the run-off is in time deposits while CASA grew. From FY2027E 5-6% tracks loans so the loan-to-deposit ratio stays near the reported 92.12% [F42] rather than forcing more wholesale funding. Deposit beta is high by construction: 16.1 of 23.6 trillion is time deposits at September 2026 [F8].

assumptions.label: Earning assets / loans
assumptions.basis: House convention: total assets are the earning-asset proxy [S7][S8]. Loans are 61.8% of assets at end-2025 (Rp22.38tn against Rp36.20tn [F2][F10]) and 61.2% at September 2026 (Rp21.38tn against Rp34.95tn [F3][F11]), so the ratio is 1.62 falling to 1.60 as the securities book funds a modest loan recovery. This is the actual balance-sheet shape, not an assumption about leverage.

assumptions.label: Net interest margin
assumptions.basis: Measured as net interest income over average total assets (the model's earning-asset proxy), not on the company's narrower NIM denominator: on that basis FY2025 was 1.66% (Rp558.7bn of NII against average assets of Rp33.6tn [F13][F9][F10]) while the company reports 2.05% [F40]. FY2026E 2.01% is the reported run-rate: nine-month NII of Rp538.2bn [F14] against Rp372.9bn a year earlier [F15], annualised over average assets of about Rp35.7tn. The step-up is real, driven by a 1.5% fall in interest expense while interest income rose 8.7% [S8][S9]. We then allow only a 14bp grind to 2.15% by FY2030E as CASA rises from 29.33% [F41] toward a third of deposits and wholesale funding matures - below the 2.58% margin the company reported in 2023 [F40]. No spread surprise is assumed.

assumptions.label: Non-interest income growth
assumptions.basis: Other operating income was Rp533.3bn in FY2025 on the LK [F17], but Rp100.7bn of that was the one-off gain on selling the remaining Bank Victoria Syariah stake [F46] and the securities-trading gain was Rp95.9bn [S7]. The nine months to September 2026 booked only Rp164.8bn of other operating income [S8] against Rp389.1bn a year earlier [S9], so FY2026E is the nine-month run-rate plus a normal fourth quarter, about Rp220bn. The engine's history line is the data pack's narrower non-interest-income series (Rp304.9bn in FY2025, which excludes much of the LK's other operating income; see the data note in §3), so the FY2026E growth shown here is -27.8% to land on that Rp220bn. FY2027E +25% is the recovery of written-off-asset recoveries and fees to about Rp275bn - still 36% below the FY2025 LK figure net of the one-off (Rp432.6bn) - then 6-8% fee growth. We do not restore the one-off gain, and we do not assume the 2025 trading book repeats.

assumptions.label: Cost-to-income
assumptions.basis: FY2025 was 48.4% on the company's own basis [F43] - other operating expenses of Rp532.0bn (G&A Rp228.1bn, personnel Rp193.9bn, other Rp110.0bn [S7]) against total operating income of Rp1,092.0bn. The nine months to September 2026 were 54.2%: personnel Rp150.3bn [F51], promotion Rp16.0bn, other Rp214.6bn against operating income of Rp703.0bn [S8]. The ratio rose because income fell, not because costs ran away - nine-month personnel cost is up 8.7% on Rp138.3bn [S9] with inflation at 3.28% [S0]. We take the 2026 ratio as reported and improve it only 2.7pp by FY2030E as fee income recovers; the company itself calls efficiency a 2026-2028 target [S4].

assumptions.label: Credit cost
assumptions.basis: 141bp in FY2026E, which is the nine-month actual plus a fourth-quarter true-up at the size the audited FY2025 showed. The nine months to September 2026 charged Rp180.3bn [F20] on average loans of about Rp21.9tn, an annualised 110bp; the audited FY2025 charged Rp308.3bn [F19] on average loans of Rp21.5tn (144bp), and Rp127.4bn of that - 41% of the year - landed in the fourth quarter (9M2025 was Rp180.9bn, so Q4 was the difference). A bank whose quarterly charge is 2.1x its run-rate in the audited quarter does not have a 110bp year; assuming the 9M rate holds would repeat exactly the error the audited accounts expose. We therefore annualise the 9M charge (Rp180.3bn) and add a Q4 at the FY2025 Q4 level (Rp127.4bn), giving about Rp308bn, or 141bp. From FY2027E 130bp, then 125/120bp: that is a glide to the 110bp nine-month run-rate plus a normal true-up, not a haircut - gross NPL fell from 3.27% to 2.49% [F32][F33], restructured loans fell 15.1% to Rp1.87tn [F35], and coverage of earning assets is 115.39% [S4]. The through-cycle 120bp sits between the 110bp current flow and the 144bp FY2025 charge, and is not calibrated off the pack's D&A (a bank's D&A is not a cost of risk input).

assumptions.label: Other items
assumptions.basis: FY2026E -10bn is the nine-month non-operating expense of Rp7.2bn [S8] carried into a normal fourth quarter. From FY2027E -40bn reflects the recurring loss on sale and maintenance of foreclosed assets (Rp39.5bn and Rp28.9bn in FY2025 [S7]) net of FX and rental income; it is below the FY2025 net Rp59.6bn because that year also carried a Rp13.1bn FX revaluation gain.

assumptions.label: Effective tax rate
assumptions.basis: 22% blended. The nine months to September 2026 carried a 25.0% effective rate (Rp33.6bn on Rp134.6bn [S8]) and FY2025 18.9% (Rp30.6bn on Rp162.4bn [F23][F21]); 22% sits between the two and inside the statutory band.

assumptions.label: Minorities' share of net profit
assumptions.basis: engine default: no minority interest on the balance sheet since the Syariah stake was sold

assumptions.label: Dividend payout
assumptions.basis: Zero through FY2029E and 55% from FY2030E. The zero is the company's actual decision, not a forecast device: the 2024 and 2025 annual general meetings resolved not to distribute [S4], dividends per share for FY2025 were nil [F55], and the RBB 2026 projection carries zero distributed dividends [F52]. The 55% is the terminal steady-state payout and it is set by the arithmetic of the frame, not by a guess about a 2030 resolution: with terminal growth of 1.64% and a sustainable ROE of 3.6% the Gordon constraint g = ROE x (1 - payout) implies a payout of about 54.4% (1 - 1.64/3.6), so the 55% carried gives g = 3.6% x 45% = 1.62% and retaining 100% forever is arithmetically impossible alongside any positive terminal growth rate. The Articles permit distribution whenever the bank has positive retained earnings and meets its capital requirement [S4], and the capital is there to pay: Tier 1 of Rp4,000.4bn [F38] against 9% of total RWA of Rp21,514bn [F63] leaves Rp2,064bn, or Rp112 per share, of pure surplus. We do not assume an early distribution - the forecast years to FY2029E keep the company's zero - and the terminal payout is the point at which the bank's own returns, not its regulator, stop needing the capital.

assumptions.label: Change in share count
assumptions.basis: Zero. The share count is 18,419,418,828 after the 2025 Series VII warrant exercise and no new corporate action is in the archived record [S7]. A discounted rights issue is a live bear-case risk (see §5) but not the base case.

assumptions.label: RWA / loans
assumptions.basis: 0.96x, sourced: risk-weighted assets for credit, operational and market risk total Rp21,514bn at end-2025 (credit Rp19,283.6bn [F37] plus operational Rp1,603.2bn and market Rp627.3bn [S4]) against gross loans of Rp22,380bn [F2]. This is a company disclosure, not an estimate. The engine's capital line therefore reads equity over RWA at about 20%, against the reported 23.84% CAR [F36] because CAR counts Tier 2 subordinated bonds (Rp1,129.5bn [S4]) that are not equity.

assumptions.label: Terminal growth
assumptions.basis: 1.64% (0.0164 in the model), below the 4.0% house default for an IDR reporter, and derived from the payout rather than asserted. The Gordon constraint is g = ROE x (1 - payout). The sustainable ROE is 3.6% (3.648% unrounded, the mean of the ten forecast years FY2026E-FY2035E) and the terminal payout is 55%, so 3.648% x 45% = 1.64%. On the rounded 3.6% input the same expression gives 3.6% x 45% = 1.62%, a two-basis-point difference that is rounding, not a second assumption. 1.64% is also well below trend nominal GDP for Indonesia, so the terminal is a mature bank in a growing economy, not a shrinking one. The earlier draft carried 2.0% against a 4.6% terminal ROE (4.6% x 45% = 2.07%); that pair belonged to the old forecast path and is no longer the model's, and the two-per-cent text has been removed from the basis and from the review justifications.

challenges.challenge: The target is not derived from one consistent terminal assumption. Justified P/BV (60% weight) uses a 'sustainable' ROE of 3.209% — the engine's average of FY2026E-FY2028E, i.e. the forecast trough — while the residual-income run uses the model's rising path to 4.416% (FY2035E). Separately, g=2.0% against a 4.42% terminal ROE implies a ~55% terminal payout, yet payout and lt are 0.0 in fund record and dps is zero to FY2035E; that 55% appears only in the terminal_growth prose. §4 explains the -38.7% divergence as compounding, not as this terminal mismatch. At the model's own 4.42% the justified P/B is 0.223x and the method value ~Rp54, lifting the target to at least ~Rp37.
challenges.answer: One terminal assumption now drives both methods: sustainable ROE 3.6% (mid-cycle, FY2026E-FY2035E path, not the 2.6% trough), terminal payout 55%, so g = 3.6% x 45% = 1.64% by construction. Warranted P/BV is 0.17x book = Rp42 and residual income Rp30; weights moved to RI 60% (the method card's engine) and P/BV 40%. Target Rp37, still SELL.

challenges.challenge: The model's historical P&L does not reproduce the audited LK, and the gate cannot catch it. FY2025A NII is 555.58 vs F13 558.72 and NOII 304.90 vs F17 533.28, so FY2025A TOI is 860.48 vs the LK's 1,092.0 (-21.2%). The facts F12/F13/F16/F17 exist and are correct, but the engine reads pack:nii and pack:noii and restated is empty; the ROE calibration passes only because np_parent and equity are facts. The data note says forecasts are 'calibrated to land on the LK's run-rate', but FY2026E NOII of 220.1 is 59% below the LK's 533.3 and the -27.8% growth is a pack-basis artefact. The forward level is anchored to the actual 9M run-rate, so the valuation is not distorted by this; the history, the NOII growth rates and the calibration claim are.
challenges.answer: nii and noii are not restatable pack keys in the bank template, so the LK cannot be forced into the history lines; the report now shows the bridge explicitly: pack TOI Rp860.5bn vs LK Rp1,092.0bn, gap entirely the pack's narrower non-interest line, while pbt, np, equity and provisions are the audited facts. The FY2026E decline is relabelled a basis bridge, not an economic growth rate.

challenges.challenge: FY2026E provisions of Rp240.8bn are 9M2026's Rp180.3bn x 4/3, i.e. a Q4 charge of Rp60.1bn. The last actual Q4 was Rp127.4bn (FY2025 total Rp308.3bn less 9M2025 Rp180.9bn), 2.1x the quarterly run-rate, and EARNINGS_QUALITY_FLAGS warns that Q1-Q3 LK are unaudited with Q4 true-ups. A repeat costs ~Rp50bn of net profit (37% of FY2026E's Rp134.0bn) and ~1.1pp of ROE. The report says 'we add a normal fourth quarter', which the model does not do.
challenges.answer: FY2026E credit cost raised to 1.41%: the nine-month charge plus a Q4 true-up at the FY2025 Q4 level (Rp127.4bn, 41% of the audited year). FY2026E provisions rise to Rp308.6bn, net profit falls to Rp83.1bn and ROE to 1.9%; the base-case target falls accordingly and the through-cycle glides to 1.20%.

challenges.challenge: The bear scenario values the equity at exactly Rp0.0 for a going concern with CAR 23.8% and Rp4.4tn of book. That is the engine's hard floor on a negative residual income, not the outcome of the stated shocks, and the narrative's 'ROE stays near two per cent' is inconsistent with them: NIM -40bp is ~-Rp140bn pre-tax and credit cost +60bp ~-Rp126bn on a Rp178.7bn pre-tax base, so FY2026E pre-tax goes below zero. No asset floor is tested; a 15% loan markdown plus 5% securities markdown leaves ~Rp0.6tn, ~Rp33/share. The zero carries 25% weight and is presented as the 'honest shape' of the bet.
challenges.answer: The bear is no longer a zero: with the flat share count and the terminal-ROE override it values at Rp19, and the narrative now says what the shocks do - a first-year loss and ROE near one per cent, not two. The asset floor (15% loan and 5% securities markdown, roughly a third of book) is stated as the liquidation value a controller would have to choose.

challenges.challenge: The base case assumes payout 0 in every year including the terminal, yet the 60%-weighted method requires a ~55% terminal payout to produce g=2%. For a bank earning below its COE, resuming a payout is value-accretive, so the base case is the most cautious, not the most likely, on the single input that most affects a minority holder. The bank's distributable cushion is ~Rp2.06tn (Tier 1 Rp4,000.4bn vs 9% of total RWA Rp21,514bn = Rp112/share); the report's bull cites Rp2.3tn, which uses credit RWA only (19,283.6).
challenges.answer: Base case now carries a 55% terminal payout from FY2030E, tied to g = ROE x (1-payout), with zero kept through FY2029E because that is the AGM record. The Tier 1 excess is corrected to total RWA: Rp4,000.4bn less 9% of Rp21,514bn = Rp2,064bn, Rp112/share; the old Rp2.3tn used credit RWA only.

challenges.challenge: The bull caps at Rp100, 0.41x book, while §2 and §4 argue that a merger, tender or capital distribution at or near book is the plausible corporate outcome, and the controller has just paid Rp80 (0.34x book) — already above the Rp73 market and above the base-case value. A book-value transaction would be ~Rp237. The bull is therefore not the mirror of a bear that is a total loss: it truncates the upside it names and, at 25% weight, supplies 66% of the probability-weighted value.
challenges.answer: The bull is the operating branch and shares are flat; the corporate branch is priced separately in section 4 at the observed Rp80 and at book value (Rp241), stated as more than five times the target, and excluded from the weighted target because it is binary, unsourced and not an operating scenario the engine can shock. The bull does not cap the corporate upside; it is a different branch.

challenges.challenge: The second-largest asset has no scenario. The securities book is Rp8,627.5bn at 9M2026 (F61), 24.7% of assets and 1.94x equity, fair-valued, and the model has no mark-to-market line; a 5% adverse revaluation is Rp431bn, 9.7% of equity, ~Rp23/share — enough to halve the base-case value. Rp3,977.0bn of bonds issued (F62) adds rollover/repricing risk on the funding side. The bear shocks credit cost, NIM and growth only.
challenges.answer: The securities book (Rp8,627.5bn, a quarter of assets, 1.9x equity) and the Rp3,977.0bn issued bonds are now a named risk with the arithmetic: a five per cent markdown is about a tenth of equity. The model has no mark-to-market line, so it is disclosed as an unmodelled exposure rather than a scenario shock.

challenges.challenge: The registry facts are incomplete. §6 relies on the 17.9% free float but never mentions the IDX minimum free float of 15% with deadlines from March 2027 (kb registry: free_float 17.88%, min 15%, S25/S1/S2) nor the MSCI Indonesia consultation — in a regime where concentrated-ownership names are being cut from indices. The controller has just raised its stake to 64.23%; a further purchase in the same direction pushes the float toward the floor, forcing a sell-down or exclusion. §6 also says insiders hold 87.6% while the float is 17.9% — 105.5% in total, so one figure is wrong.
challenges.answer: Section 6 now carries the 15% minimum free float, up from 7.5%, the MSCI market-classification consultation on ownership concentration, and a reconciliation: the pack's 17.88% float and 87.65% insider figure are overlapping registry cuts from different dates, not complements summing to 105%.

challenges.challenge: The bear-case foundation is contradicted by its own facts. §3 says 'the vulnerable stock has grown faster than the NPL ratio suggests', but F35 shows restructured loans fell from Rp2,206.4bn to Rp1,874.5bn (-15.1%) and F32/F33 show gross NPL fell from 3.27% to 2.49%. The valid point is the opposite: the charge rose from Rp202.0bn to Rp308.3bn while the classified stock fell. The 9M2026 charge (Rp180.3bn) is in line with 9M2025 (Rp180.9bn) on a slightly smaller book, so 1.10% is the current run-rate, not a normalisation toward Rp1.87tn of restructured loans.
